---
title: "Fundamentals of Atomic Layer Deposition"
---

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## Learning outcomes
After this chapter you should be able to:

1. State the operational definition of ALD and design an experiment that tests it.
2. Estimate the exposure needed to saturate a planar surface from kinetic gas theory.
3. Interpret growth-per-cycle (GPC) versus temperature data critically, including where the "ALD window" idea breaks down.
4. Explain why a saturated half-cycle deposits only a fraction of a monolayer, and convert a GPC into a coverage.
5. Recognize non-linear initial growth and correct thickness-based GPC estimates for it.
:::

## What makes a process ALD? {#sec-what-makes-ald}

Atomic layer deposition builds a film by exposing a surface to two (or more) reactants **one at a time**, with a purge or evacuation between them. Each exposure is a gas–surface reaction that stops by itself once the available surface sites are used up [@George2010; @Johnson2014].

The defining property is **self-limitation**, not the cycle structure. Plenty of pulsed processes have an A–purge–B–purge sequence but are not ALD, because one of the steps keeps depositing material as the dose increases. The practical test is therefore experimental:

> For each half-reaction, the growth per cycle (GPC) must reach a plateau as that reactant's dose increases, and must not depend on purge length once the purge is adequate.

Any other characteristic (conformality, digital thickness control, low pinhole density) follows from this property. None of them can stand in for testing it.

## The model system: TMA/H~2~O → Al~2~O~3~

The trimethylaluminum (TMA)/water process is the most-studied ALD chemistry and is the usual reference point [@Puurunen2005]. In simplified form, the two half-reactions on a hydroxylated surface (asterisks denote surface species) are:

$$
\text{A:}\quad \|\!-\!\text{OH}^* + \text{Al(CH}_3)_3 \rightarrow \|\!-\!\text{O–Al(CH}_3)_2^* + \text{CH}_4
$$ {#eq-tma}

$$
\text{B:}\quad \|\!-\!\text{Al–CH}_3^* + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \|\!-\!\text{Al–OH}^* + \text{CH}_4
$$ {#eq-water}

Reaction A consumes hydroxyls and leaves a methyl-terminated surface that does not react further with TMA. Reaction B restores the hydroxyl termination. The overall reaction, 2 Al(CH~3~)~3~ + 3 H~2~O → Al~2~O~3~ + 6 CH~4~, is strongly exothermic, which partly explains why the process is so robust [@George2010].

Step through one cycle below to see how the two half-reactions alternate. The diagram is a cartoon: each dot is an atom, but sizes and spacings are not to scale.

::: {.sim-box}
[Simulation 2.1: One ALD cycle of TMA/H~2~O]{.sim-title}

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof cyc = {
  const wrap = html`<div class="cycle-controls">
    <button type="button" data-a="prev" aria-label="Previous step">◀ Back</button>
    <button type="button" data-a="play" aria-label="Play or pause">▶ Play</button>
    <button type="button" data-a="next" aria-label="Next step">Next ▶</button>
    <button type="button" data-a="reset" aria-label="Reset to start">Reset</button>
  </div>`;
  let v = 0, timer = null;
  const playBtn = wrap.querySelector('[data-a="play"]');
  const set = (x) => {
    v = Math.max(0, Math.min(x, 400));
    wrap.value = v;
    wrap.dispatchEvent(new Event("input", {bubbles: true}));
  };
  const stop = () => { clearInterval(timer); timer = null; playBtn.textContent = "▶ Play"; };
  wrap.value = v;
  wrap.setTo = (x) => { stop(); set(x); };
  wrap.addEventListener("click", (e) => {
    const a = e.target.closest("button")?.dataset.a;
    if (a === "next") { stop(); set(v + 1); }
    if (a === "prev") { stop(); set(v - 1); }
    if (a === "reset") { stop(); set(0); }
    if (a === "play") {
      if (timer) stop();
      else { playBtn.textContent = "❚❚ Pause"; set(v + 1); timer = setInterval(() => set(v + 1), 2200); }
    }
  });
  invalidation.then(stop);
  return wrap;
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
cycleFigure = {
  const GPC = 1.1;                                     // Å, for the thickness readout
  const step = cyc === 0 ? -1 : (cyc - 1) % 4;         // -1 = starting surface
  const cycleNo = cyc === 0 ? 1 : Math.floor((cyc - 1) / 4) + 1;
  const done = Math.floor(cyc / 4);                    // completed cycles
  const steps = [
    {name: "Pulse TMA", short: "TMA", gas: "Al(CH₃)₃"},
    {name: "Purge", short: "Purge", gas: "N₂"},
    {name: "Pulse H₂O", short: "H₂O", gas: "H₂O"},
    {name: "Purge", short: "Purge", gas: "N₂"}
  ];
  const red = "#E91C24", dark = "#4D4D4D", grey = "#8C8C8C", light = "#EDEDED";

  // --- atoms --------------------------------------------------------------
  const atom = (x, y, el, r) => {
    const s = {Al: [dark, "white", 11], O: [red, "white", 9], C: ["#000", "white", 9],
               H: ["white", "#000", 5.5], N: [grey, "white", 7]}[el];
    const rr = r ?? s[2];
    const lab = el === "H" ? "" : `<text x="${x}" y="${y + 3.5}" text-anchor="middle" font-size="${el === "Al" ? 10 : 9.5}" fill="${s[1]}" font-weight="600">${el === "C" ? "C" : el}</text>`;
    return `<circle cx="${x}" cy="${y}" r="${rr}" fill="${s[0]}" stroke="#000" stroke-width="${el === "H" ? 1 : 0.8}"/>${lab}`;
  };
  const bond = (x1, y1, x2, y2) => `<line x1="${x1}" y1="${y1}" x2="${x2}" y2="${y2}" stroke="#000" stroke-width="1.4"/>`;
  // Carbon with explicit H atoms. A methyl's three H point away from the atom it is bonded to (ax, ay).
  const withH = (x, y, angles) => {
    const hs = angles.map(a => [x + 14 * Math.cos(a), y + 14 * Math.sin(a)]);
    return hs.map(([hx, hy]) => bond(x, y, hx, hy)).join("") + hs.map(([hx, hy]) => atom(hx, hy, "H")).join("") + atom(x, y, "C");
  };
  const methyl = (x, y, ax, ay) => {
    const d = Math.atan2(y - ay, x - ax), s = 1.1;
    return withH(x, y, [d - s, d, d + s]);
  };
  const tma = (x, y) => bond(x, y, x - 20, y + 12) + bond(x, y, x + 20, y + 12) + bond(x, y, x, y - 23) +
    methyl(x - 20, y + 12, x, y) + methyl(x + 20, y + 12, x, y) + methyl(x, y - 23, x, y) + atom(x, y, "Al");
  const water = (x, y) => bond(x, y, x - 10, y + 8) + bond(x, y, x + 10, y + 8) + atom(x - 10, y + 8, "H") + atom(x + 10, y + 8, "H") + atom(x, y, "O");
  const methane = (x, y) => withH(x, y, [0.785, 2.356, 3.927, 5.498]);
  const n2 = (x, y) => atom(x - 6, y, "N", 6) + atom(x + 6, y, "N", 6);

  // --- reactor geometry -----------------------------------------------------
  const X0 = 250, X1 = 720, GAS_TOP = 30, SUB_TOP = 330;
  const filmPx = Math.min(done, 12) * 5;               // drawn film thickness
  const surf = SUB_TOP - filmPx;                       // top of film
  const sites = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5].map(i => 285 + i * 78);
  // Adsorbed species after the TMA pulse. "di": TMA on one –OH (–O–Al(CH₃)₂);
  // "mono": TMA bridging two –OH (–O)₂Al(CH₃); "oh": –OH shielded by neighbouring methyls.
  const species = [
    {type: "di", at: [0]}, {type: "mono", at: [1, 2]}, {type: "di", at: [3]},
    {type: "oh", at: [4]}, {type: "di", at: [5]}
  ];

  // surface state after the current step
  const state = step === 0 || step === 1 ? "Me" : step === 2 ? "OH" : "bare";
  const lig = (x, y, ax, ay) => state === "Me" ? methyl(x, y, ax, ay) : bond(x, y, x, y - 16) + atom(x, y - 16, "H") + atom(x, y, "O");
  const tags = {di: "dimethyl", mono: "monomethyl", oh: "shielded –OH"};
  let surface = "";
  const y0 = surf - 9, yAl = y0 - 26;
  species.forEach(sp => {
    const xs = sp.at.map(i => sites[i]);
    if (state === "bare" || sp.type === "oh") {
      xs.forEach(x => { surface += bond(x, y0, x, y0 - 16) + atom(x, y0 - 16, "H") + atom(x, y0, "O"); });
    } else if (sp.type === "di") {
      const x = xs[0];
      surface += bond(x, y0, x, yAl) + bond(x, yAl, x - 16, yAl - 18) + bond(x, yAl, x + 16, yAl - 18) +
        lig(x - 16, yAl - 18, x, yAl) + lig(x + 16, yAl - 18, x, yAl) + atom(x, yAl, "Al") + atom(x, y0, "O");
    } else {
      const xm = (xs[0] + xs[1]) / 2;
      surface += xs.map(x => bond(x, y0, xm, yAl)).join("") + bond(xm, yAl, xm, yAl - 20) +
        lig(xm, yAl - 20, xm, yAl) + atom(xm, yAl, "Al") + xs.map(x => atom(x, y0, "O")).join("");
    }
    if (step === 0 || step === 1) {
      const xm = xs.reduce((u, v) => u + v, 0) / xs.length;
      surface += `<text x="${xm}" y="${surf - (sp.type === "oh" ? 52 : 82)}" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="${dark}">${tags[sp.type]}</text>`;
    }
  });

  // gas phase
  const P = [[300, 88], [395, 130], [480, 96], [560, 140], [655, 95], [345, 185], [615, 195], [500, 205]];
  const g = (f, idx) => idx.map((k, j) => `<g class="drift" style="animation-delay:${-j * 0.7}s">${f(P[k][0], P[k][1])}</g>`).join("");
  let gas = "";
  if (step === 0) gas = g(tma, [0, 2, 4, 5]) + g(methane, [1, 3, 6, 7]);
  if (step === 1 || step === 3) gas = g(n2, [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]);
  if (step === 2) gas = g(water, [0, 2, 4, 5, 7]) + g(methane, [1, 3, 6]);

  const flowLabel = step === -1 ? "" : steps[step].gas;
  const reactor = `
    <rect x="${X0}" y="${GAS_TOP}" width="${X1 - X0}" height="${SUB_TOP - GAS_TOP}" fill="#FFFFFF" stroke="${grey}"/>
    ${step >= 0 ? `<g class="flow"><path d="M${X0 + 8} 22 h60" stroke="${step % 2 ? grey : red}" stroke-width="3" marker-end="url(#arr)"/></g>
       <text x="${X0 + 8}" y="16" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="${step % 2 ? dark : red}">in: ${flowLabel}</text>
       <text x="${X1 - 8}" y="16" font-size="12" text-anchor="end" fill="${dark}">to pump →</text>` : ""}
    <rect x="${X0}" y="${SUB_TOP}" width="${X1 - X0}" height="28" fill="${light}" stroke="${grey}"/>
    <text x="${X1 - 8}" y="${SUB_TOP + 18}" font-size="11" text-anchor="end" fill="${dark}">substrate</text>
    ${filmPx ? `<rect x="${X0}" y="${surf}" width="${X1 - X0}" height="${filmPx}" fill="#F4B6B8" stroke="${red}" stroke-width="0.6"/>` : ""}
    ${gas}${surface}`;

  // --- cycle ring -------------------------------------------------------------
  const cx = 115, cy = 150, R = 82, w = 26;
  const arc = (k) => {
    const a0 = -Math.PI / 2 + k * Math.PI / 2 + 0.06, a1 = a0 + Math.PI / 2 - 0.12;
    const p = (a, r) => [cx + r * Math.cos(a), cy + r * Math.sin(a)];
    const [x0, y0] = p(a0, R), [x1, y1] = p(a1, R), [x2, y2] = p(a1, R - w), [x3, y3] = p(a0, R - w);
    const on = k === step;
    const fill = on ? red : k % 2 ? light : "#D6D6D6";
    const am = (a0 + a1) / 2, [lx, ly] = p(am, R + 16);
    const anchor = Math.cos(am) > 0.2 ? "start" : Math.cos(am) < -0.2 ? "end" : "middle";
    return `<g class="ring-step" data-k="${k}" style="cursor:pointer">
      <path d="M${x0},${y0} A${R},${R} 0 0 1 ${x1},${y1} L${x2},${y2} A${R - w},${R - w} 0 0 0 ${x3},${y3} Z" fill="${fill}" stroke="#fff" stroke-width="2"/>
      <text x="${lx}" y="${ly + 4}" text-anchor="${anchor}" font-size="13.5" font-weight="${on ? 700 : 400}" fill="${on ? red : "#000"}">${k + 1}. ${steps[k].short}</text></g>`;
  };
  const ring = [0, 1, 2, 3].map(arc).join("") + `
    <text x="${cx}" y="${cy - 6}" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" font-weight="600">Cycle ${cycleNo}</text>
    <text x="${cx}" y="${cy + 13}" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="${dark}">${done} done · ≈ ${(done * GPC).toFixed(1)} Å</text>`;

  // --- valve timing strip ----------------------------------------------------------
  const TX = 250, TW = 470, TY = 385, seg = TW / 4;
  const trace = (row, k, label, col) => {
    const y = TY + row * 30, hi = y - 12;
    const xs = TX + k * seg;
    return `<text x="${TX - 8}" y="${y + 2}" text-anchor="end" font-size="12.5" fill="${dark}">${label}</text>
      <path d="M${TX},${y} H${xs + 6} V${hi} H${xs + seg - 6} V${y} H${TX + TW}" fill="none" stroke="${col}" stroke-width="2"/>`;
  };
  const timing = `
    ${step >= 0 ? `<rect x="${TX + step * seg}" y="${TY - 24}" width="${seg}" height="56" fill="${red}" opacity="0.1"/>` : ""}
    ${trace(0, 0, "TMA valve", red)}${trace(1, 2, "H₂O valve", dark)}
    ${steps.map((s, k) => `<text x="${TX + k * seg + seg / 2}" y="${TY + 48}" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12.5" fill="${k === step ? red : dark}" font-weight="${k === step ? 700 : 400}">${s.name}</text>`).join("")}`;

  const key = `<g transform="translate(10,458)" font-size="12.5" fill="${dark}">
    <text x="0" y="0">Key:</text>
    ${atom(45, -4, "Al")}<text x="60" y="0">Al</text>
    ${atom(95, -4, "O")}<text x="108" y="0">O</text>
    ${methyl(152, -2, 152, 12)}<text x="176" y="0">methyl group (CH₃)</text>
    ${atom(302, -4, "H")}<text x="313" y="0">H</text>
    ${n2(345, -4)}<text x="360" y="0">N₂ purge gas</text>
    <rect x="465" y="-11" width="16" height="10" fill="#F4B6B8" stroke="${red}" stroke-width="0.6"/><text x="487" y="0">deposited Al₂O₃</text></g>`;
  const wrap = document.createElement("div");
  wrap.innerHTML = `<svg viewBox="0 0 740 470" width="100%" style="max-width:820px" role="img" aria-label="ALD cycle diagram, step ${step + 1}">
    <defs><marker id="arr" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="8" refY="5" markerWidth="6" markerHeight="6" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z" fill="context-stroke"/></marker></defs>
    ${ring}${reactor}${timing}${key}</svg>`;
  wrap.querySelectorAll(".ring-step").forEach(el => el.addEventListener("click", () => {
    const k = +el.dataset.k;
    viewof cyc.setTo(4 * (cycleNo - 1) + k + 1);
  }));
  return wrap;
}
```

```{ojs}
{

  const text = [
    ["Starting surface", "A hydroxylated (–OH-terminated) substrate. Press <b>Next</b> or <b>Play</b>, or click a step in the ring."],
    ["1. Pulse TMA", "Al(CH₃)₃ reacts with surface –OH groups in two ways. Reacting with one –OH gives a <b>dimethyl</b> species, ‖–OH* + Al(CH₃)₃ → ‖–O–Al(CH₃)₂* + CH₄. Reacting with two neighbouring –OH groups gives a <b>monomethyl</b> species, 2 ‖–OH* + Al(CH₃)₃ → (‖–O)₂–Al(CH₃)* + 2 CH₄. The balance between the two sets how many methyl groups go on to the water step. Once the reachable –OH groups are used up, the methyl-terminated surface does not react with more TMA, so the half-reaction stops by itself. Some –OH groups stay unreacted because neighbouring methyl groups shield them (steric hindrance). Excess TMA and CH₄ remain in the gas."],
    ["2. Purge", "Inert gas sweeps out unreacted TMA and the CH₄ by-product. If the purge is too short, TMA meets water in the gas phase in the next step and CVD growth adds to the film."],
    ["3. Pulse H₂O", "Water converts every remaining surface methyl group, on both dimethyl and monomethyl species, to a hydroxyl: ‖–Al–CH₃* + H₂O → ‖–Al–OH* + CH₄. The surface is hydroxylated again and ready for the next TMA pulse."],
    ["4. Purge", "Water and CH₄ are removed. The cycle is complete, and the new Al–O material is now part of the film (pink). Each cycle adds about one GPC (≈ 1.1 Å), well below one monolayer of Al₂O₃."]
  ][step + 1];
  return html`<div class="map-card"><div class="map-card-title">${text[0]}</div><div>${html([text[1]])}</div></div>`;
}
```

::: {.assumptions}
**Assumptions.** Idealized chemistry: TMA binds to one –OH (dimethyl) or two –OH (monomethyl); dissociation onto Al–O bridges is left out, and water removes every remaining methyl group. The mix of dimethyl, monomethyl and unreacted sites is chosen for illustration; in reality it depends on temperature and –OH density. After each completed cycle the new material is drawn as a uniform film layer, and the thickness readout uses a fixed GPC of 1.1 Å. Pulse and purge times on the valve trace are schematic.
:::
:::

Two points are worth stating early, because students often get them wrong:

- **GPC is a fraction of a monolayer.** For TMA/H~2~O, a typical GPC is about 1 Å, which is well below the thickness of one "layer" of Al~2~O~3~. The amount of metal adsorbed per cycle is limited by **steric hindrance** from the ligands that remain after chemisorption and by the **number of reactive sites**. Which of the two dominates depends on the chemistry and the temperature [@Puurunen2005] (see @sec-steric).
- **Eqs. [-@eq-tma]–[-@eq-water] are idealized.** In reality, TMA can react with one or two hydroxyls, and it can also dissociate onto Al–O bridges. The ratio between these pathways sets how many methyl groups survive into step B. This is why the hydroxyl density, and hence the temperature, controls the GPC.

## Steric crowding: why one cycle is not one monolayer {#sec-steric}

A saturated TMA half-cycle does not deposit a monolayer of Al~2~O~3~. Each chemisorbed fragment keeps one or two methyl groups, and these take up much more room on the surface than a bare aluminum atom would [@Barry2022]. The methyls cover neighbouring –OH groups so that no further TMA molecule can reach them. The half-reaction saturates when every remaining –OH is either consumed or shielded. That point comes long before the surface holds a full layer of aluminum. In other words, a saturated layer of chemisorbed precursor is not a monolayer of the target film [@Barry2022; @Puurunen2005].

There are two ways the coverage can be limited:

- **Site-limited.** If –OH groups are sparse, TMA can reach all of them. The amount of Al per cycle is then set by the hydroxyl density.
- **Sterically limited.** If –OH groups are dense, the ligands of the first fragments to land block the rest. The amount of Al per cycle is then set by the size of the fragments, not by the number of sites.

Which regime applies depends on the precursor and the temperature, because the hydroxyl density falls as the surface dehydroxylates at higher temperature [@Puurunen2005].

The simulation below drops TMA molecules at random onto a 10 nm × 10 nm patch of hydroxylated surface. Each molecule that lands on a free, unshielded –OH chemisorbs, either as a dimethyl species (one –OH) or, if a second free –OH is close by, as a monomethyl species (two –OH). Set the methyl diameter to zero to switch off steric hindrance and see the site-limited case.

::: {.sim-box}
[Simulation 2.2: Steric crowding during the TMA half-cycle]{.sim-title}

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof ohDens = Inputs.range([2, 12], {value: 8, step: 0.5, label: "–OH density (nm⁻²)"})
viewof meD = Inputs.range([0, 4.5], {value: 3.5, step: 0.1, label: "Methyl group diameter (Å)"})
viewof pBi = Inputs.range([0, 1], {value: 0.4, step: 0.05, label: "Probability of reacting with two –OH"})
viewof expo = Inputs.range([0, 6], {value: 6, step: 0.05, label: "TMA exposure (arrivals per –OH)"})
viewof reseed = Inputs.button("New random surface")
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
steric = {
  reseed;                                            // re-run on button press
  const L = 100;                                     // patch size, Å
  let seed = (Math.random() * 2 ** 32) >>> 0;
  const rnd = () => {                                // mulberry32
    seed |= 0; seed = (seed + 0x6D2B79F5) | 0;
    let t = Math.imul(seed ^ (seed >>> 15), 1 | seed);
    t = (t + Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 7), 61 | t)) ^ t;
    return ((t ^ (t >>> 14)) >>> 0) / 4294967296;
  };
  const N = Math.round(ohDens * L * L / 100);
  const sites = d3.range(N).map(() => ({x: rnd() * L, y: rnd() * L, used: false}));
  const wrap = v => v - L * Math.round(v / L);
  const dist = (a, b) => Math.hypot(wrap(a.x - b.x), wrap(a.y - b.y));
  // neighbour lists for bifunctional reaction (second –OH within 3.5 Å)
  const nb = sites.map((s, i) => sites.map((t, j) => j).filter(j => j !== i && dist(s, sites[j]) < 3.5));
  const dDi = meD * Math.SQRT2, dMono = meD;         // footprint diameters
  const frags = [];
  const fits = (c, d) => frags.every(f => dist(c, f) >= (d + f.d) / 2);
  const total = Math.round(6 * N), curve = [{e: 0, al: 0}];
  for (let k = 1; k <= total; k++) {
    const i = Math.floor(rnd() * N), s = sites[i];
    if (!s.used) {
      let placed = false;
      if (rnd() < pBi) {
        const free = nb[i].filter(j => !sites[j].used);
        if (free.length) {
          const j = free.reduce((a, b) => dist(s, sites[a]) < dist(s, sites[b]) ? a : b);
          const t = sites[j];
          const c = {x: (s.x + wrap(t.x - s.x) / 2 + L) % L, y: (s.y + wrap(t.y - s.y) / 2 + L) % L};
          if (fits(c, dMono)) {
            s.used = t.used = true;
            frags.push({...c, d: dMono, me: 1, k, a: s, b: t});
            placed = true;
          }
        }
      }
      if (!placed && fits(s, dDi)) { s.used = true; frags.push({x: s.x, y: s.y, d: dDi, me: 2, k, a: s}); }
    }
    if (k % Math.max(1, Math.round(N / 20)) === 0) curve.push({e: k / N, al: frags.length});
  }
  return {L, N, sites, frags, curve};
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
stericNow = {
  const kMax = expo * steric.N;
  const frags = steric.frags.filter(f => f.k <= kMax);
  const used = new Set(frags.flatMap(f => f.me === 1 ? [f.a, f.b] : [f.a]));
  const area = steric.L * steric.L / 100;            // nm²
  const al = frags.length / area;                    // Al nm⁻²
  const me = frags.reduce((s, f) => s + f.me, 0) / area;
  const vAl = 101.96 / (2 * 3.0 * 6.02214e23) * 1e24;// Å³ per Al at 3.0 g cm⁻³
  const gpc = al / 100 * vAl;                        // Å
  const ml = Math.cbrt(vAl);                         // Å, one "layer" of Al2O3
  return {frags, used, al, me, gpc, ml, ohUsed: used.size / steric.N,
          nMono: frags.filter(f => f.me === 1).length, nDi: frags.filter(f => f.me === 2).length};
}
```

```{ojs}
    let out = "";
    for (const dx of [-steric.L, 0, steric.L]) for (const dy of [-steric.L, 0, steric.L]) {
      const x = f.x + dx, y = f.y + dy;
      if (x > -6 && x < steric.L + 6 && y > -6 && y < steric.L + 6) out += draw(x, y);
    }
    return out;
  };
  let svg = `<rect width="${S}" height="${S}" fill="#FFFFFF" stroke="#8C8C8C"/>`;
  for (const f of stericNow.frags) {
    svg += wrapDraw(f, (x, y) => {
      const r = Math.max(f.d / 2, 0.9) * sc;
      const fill = f.me === 2 ? "#4D4D4D" : "#B3B3B3";
      return `<circle cx="${x * sc}" cy="${y * sc}" r="${r}" fill="${fill}" fill-opacity="0.55" stroke="#000" stroke-width="0.6"/>`;
    });
  }
  for (const s of steric.sites) {
    const used = stericNow.used.has(s);
    svg += `<circle cx="${s.x * sc}" cy="${s.y * sc}" r="${used ? 1.6 : 2.2}" fill="${used ? "#000" : "#E91C24"}"/>`;
  }
  const map = `<svg viewBox="0 0 ${S} ${S}" width="${S}" height="${S}" style="max-width:100%" role="img" aria-label="Top view of the surface after the TMA pulse">${svg}</svg>`;
  const legend = `<div class="map-legend" style="margin-top:0.4rem">
      <span><i style="background:#E91C24;border-color:#E91C24"></i>free –OH</span>
      <span><i style="background:#000"></i>reacted –OH</span>
      <span><i style="background:#4D4D4D;opacity:0.6"></i>dimethyl footprint</span>
      <span><i style="background:#B3B3B3"></i>monomethyl footprint</span></div>`;
  const curve = Plot.plot({
    width: width < 640 ? Math.min(width - 10, 400) : 300, height: 320, marginLeft: 50, marginBottom: 45,
    x: {label: "TMA exposure (arrivals per –OH) →", domain: [0, 6]},
    y: {label: "↑ Al adsorbed (nm⁻²)", domain: [0, Math.max(ohDens, 4) * 1.05], grid: true},
    marks: [
      Plot.ruleY([ohDens], {stroke: "#8C8C8C", strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
      Plot.text([{x: 6, y: ohDens}], {x: "x", y: "y", text: () => "every –OH reacted", textAnchor: "end", dy: -7, fill: "#4D4D4D"}),
      Plot.line(steric.curve, {x: "e", y: d => d.al / (steric.L * steric.L / 100), stroke: "#000", strokeWidth: 2}),
      Plot.dot([{x: expo, y: stericNow.al}], {x: "x", y: "y", r: 6, fill: "#E91C24"})
    ]
  });
  const box = html`<div><div style="display:flex;flex-wrap:wrap;gap:1rem;align-items:flex-start">
    <div>${html([map])}</div><div>${curve}</div></div>${html([legend])}</div>`;
  return box;
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
md`Al adsorbed: **${stericNow.al.toFixed(2)} nm⁻²** (${stericNow.nDi} dimethyl, ${stericNow.nMono} monomethyl) · –OH consumed: **${(100 * stericNow.ohUsed).toFixed(0)} %** · CH₃ left for the water step: **${stericNow.me.toFixed(2)} nm⁻²**

Implied GPC: **${stericNow.gpc.toFixed(2)} Å**, which is **${(100 * stericNow.gpc / stericNow.ml).toFixed(0)} %** of one Al₂O₃ layer (${stericNow.ml.toFixed(1)} Å). Measured TMA/H₂O processes typically give about 1.1 Å.`
```

::: {.assumptions}
**Assumptions.** Random sequential adsorption: TMA arrives at random –OH sites, sticks irreversibly where it lands, and never moves. Each fragment's footprint is a disc: a dimethyl species covers the area of two methyl groups, a monomethyl species the area of one. A molecule chemisorbs only if its footprint does not overlap an existing one. A monomethyl species forms only when a second free –OH lies within 3.5 Å. –OH groups are placed at random, and edges wrap around. TMA reaction with Al–O bridges is left out. The GPC conversion assumes each adsorbed Al ends up in Al~2~O~3~ of density 3.0 g cm^−3^.

**Where it fails.** With realistic settings the model gives 0.6–0.9 Å, below the measured ~1.1 Å. Random, irreversible adsorption is the least efficient way to pack a surface, real fragments can rearrange, and the omitted reaction with Al–O bridges adds Al without consuming –OH. Use the model for trends (how coverage responds to –OH density and ligand size), not for absolute numbers.
:::
:::

### What is "typical" coverage for TMA/H~2~O?

A useful way to express coverage is to compare the GPC with the thickness of one "layer" of the film. For Al~2~O~3~ with a density of about 3.0 g cm^−3^, the volume per Al atom is

$$
V_\text{Al} = \frac{M_{\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3}}{2\,\rho\,N_\text{A}} = \frac{101.96\ \text{g mol}^{-1}}{2 \times 3.0\ \text{g cm}^{-3} \times 6.022\times10^{23}\ \text{mol}^{-1}} \approx 28\ \text{Å}^3
$$ {#eq-val}

The cube root of this volume, about 3 Å, is a reasonable estimate of the thickness of one layer; @Barry2022 quotes about 2.9 Å. A typical TMA/H~2~O GPC of 1.1 Å therefore corresponds to:

- **About 30–40 % of a monolayer** of Al~2~O~3~ per cycle, depending on temperature and nucleation-site density [@Barry2022].
- **About 4 Al atoms per nm^2^ per cycle** (1.1 Å ÷ 28 Å^3^ ≈ 0.039 Å^−2^), compared with roughly 11 nm^−2^ for a complete layer.

So it takes about three cycles to deposit the equivalent of one layer of aluminum oxide. After the TMA pulse, the surface is a mixture of fragments that have lost one methyl group and fragments that have lost two [@Barry2022]. Their ratio sets how many methyls go on to the water step, and both the ratio and the –OH density shift with temperature. This is why the GPC of TMA/H~2~O changes with deposition temperature even though each half-reaction is self-limiting [@Puurunen2005].

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Saturation is not a monolayer
"Saturated" means the surface will take up no more precursor. It does not mean the surface is covered with a full layer of metal atoms. For almost every ALD process, a saturated half-cycle deposits a fraction of a monolayer of the final film.
:::

## Saturation and dose

How much precursor is "enough"? For a planar surface, a first estimate comes from kinetic gas theory. The impingement flux of molecules of mass $m$ at pressure $p$ and temperature $T$ is the Hertz–Knudsen flux:

$$
\Phi = \frac{p}{\sqrt{2\pi m k_\mathrm{B} T}}
$$ {#eq-flux}

If each impinging molecule reacts with probability $s$ on a free site, and there are $n_0$ reactive sites per unit area, first-order (Langmuir) kinetics give the fractional coverage after a pulse of length $t$:

$$
\theta(t) = 1 - \exp\!\left(-\frac{s\,\Phi\,t}{n_0}\right)
$$ {#eq-langmuir}

The simulation below evaluates @eq-flux and @eq-langmuir for TMA (M = 72.09 g mol^−1^) and scales the GPC by the coverage.

::: {.sim-box}
[Simulation 2.3: Saturation of a half-reaction]{.sim-title}

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof P_mTorr = Inputs.range([0.5, 100], {value: 10, step: 0.5, label: "Partial pressure (mTorr)"})
viewof T_C = Inputs.range([50, 350], {value: 200, step: 5, label: "Temperature (°C)"})
viewof logS = Inputs.range([-5, -1], {value: -3, step: 0.1, label: "log₁₀ sticking probability, s"})
viewof n0_e14 = Inputs.range([1, 10], {value: 4, step: 0.5, label: "Reactive sites (10¹⁴ cm⁻²)"})
viewof gpcSat = Inputs.range([0.2, 2], {value: 1.1, step: 0.05, label: "Saturated GPC (Å)"})
viewof tPulse = Inputs.range([0.001, 1], {value: 0.3, step: 0.001, label: "Pulse time (s)"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
satModel = {
  const kB = 1.380649e-23, NA = 6.02214076e23, M = 72.09e-3;   // TMA
  const p = P_mTorr * 0.133322;                                  // Pa
  const m = M / NA;                                              // kg
  const T = T_C + 273.15;
  const flux = p / Math.sqrt(2 * Math.PI * m * kB * T) / 1e4;    // cm^-2 s^-1
  const k = Math.pow(10, logS) * flux / (n0_e14 * 1e14);         // s^-1
  const t99 = Math.log(100) / k;
  const tMax = Math.max(3 * t99, 1.2 * tPulse);
  const pts = d3.range(0, 201).map(i => {
    const t = tMax * i / 200;
    return {t, gpc: gpcSat * (1 - Math.exp(-k * t))};
  });
  const theta = 1 - Math.exp(-k * tPulse);
  return {flux, k, t99, pts, theta, exposureL: P_mTorr * 1e-3 * tPulse / 1e-6,
          exposure99L: P_mTorr * 1e-3 * t99 / 1e-6};
}

Plot.plot({
  height: 340, marginLeft: 65, marginBottom: 50, marginTop: 30,
  x: {label: "Pulse time (s) →"},
  y: {label: "↑ GPC (Å)", domain: [0, gpcSat * 1.1], grid: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([gpcSat], {stroke: "#8C8C8C", strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
    Plot.line(satModel.pts, {x: "t", y: "gpc", stroke: "#000000", strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.ruleX([satModel.t99], {stroke: "#4D4D4D", strokeDasharray: "2,3"}),
    Plot.dot([{t: tPulse, gpc: gpcSat * satModel.theta}], {x: "t", y: "gpc", r: 6, fill: "#E91C24"})
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
md`Flux: **${satModel.flux.toExponential(2)} cm⁻² s⁻¹** · Coverage at this pulse: **${(100 * satModel.theta).toFixed(1)} %** · Exposure: **${satModel.exposureL.toFixed(0)} L**

Pulse needed for 99 % coverage (dotted line): **${satModel.t99 < 1 ? (1000 * satModel.t99).toFixed(1) + " ms" : satModel.t99.toFixed(2) + " s"}** (≈ ${satModel.exposure99L.toExponential(1)} L)`
```

::: {.assumptions}
**Assumptions:** planar substrate; ideal-gas flux at the substrate temperature; constant precursor partial pressure during the pulse; first-order Langmuir adsorption with constant $s$; GPC proportional to coverage of this half-reaction only (the other half-reaction is assumed saturated); no CVD or decomposition contribution. 1 L (Langmuir) = 10^−6^ Torr s.
:::
:::

Things to try:

- Change *s* by one decade and watch the saturation time change by a decade as well. Reported sticking probabilities vary over orders of magnitude, so a "saturating dose" taken from someone else's reactor is only a starting point.
- Notice that the model contains **no** temperature dependence of *s*. In real systems *s* is often thermally activated, which couples dose requirements to the temperature window (next section).

**High aspect ratio structures.** In a trench or pore, molecules must diffuse in, mostly in the Knudsen regime, while being consumed on the walls. The exposure needed for conformal coverage therefore grows steeply with aspect ratio: for large aspect ratios it scales roughly with the aspect ratio squared [@Gordon2003]. Doses that saturate a planar witness wafer can badly undercoat a high-aspect-ratio sample.

## The ALD window and its limits

GPC is commonly plotted against temperature, and the range over which it is approximately constant is called the **ALD window**. On either side, growth departs from the ideal for different reasons:

| Region | GPC trend | Typical cause |
|---|---|---|
| Low *T*, high GPC | ↑ | Precursor or co-reactant condensation; physisorbed water not removed by the purge |
| Low *T*, low GPC | ↓ | Insufficient thermal energy; the reaction is too slow to saturate in the pulse time |
| High *T*, high GPC | ↑ | Precursor decomposition, which adds a CVD-like, non-self-limiting component |
| High *T*, low GPC | ↓ | Desorption of chemisorbed species, or loss of reactive sites (e.g. dehydroxylation) |

::: {.sim-box}
[Simulation 2.4: A qualitative ALD window]{.sim-title}

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof Tlow = Inputs.range([50, 250], {value: 140, step: 5, label: "Lower edge (°C)"})
viewof Thigh = Inputs.range([150, 450], {value: 300, step: 5, label: "Upper edge (°C)"})
viewof slope = Inputs.range([-0.4, 0.4], {value: 0, step: 0.02, label: "GPC slope inside window (Å per 100 °C)"})
viewof lowMode = Inputs.radio(["Condensation", "Insufficient reactivity"], {value: "Insufficient reactivity", label: "Below the window"})
viewof highMode = Inputs.radio(["Decomposition", "Desorption / site loss"], {value: "Decomposition", label: "Above the window"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
windowPts = {
  const g0 = 1.0;
  const hi = Math.max(Thigh, Tlow + 20);
  const mid = (Tlow + hi) / 2;
  const inside = T => g0 + slope * (T - mid) / 100;
  const g = T => {
    if (T < Tlow) {
      const d = Tlow - T;
      return lowMode === "Condensation" ? inside(Tlow) * (1 + 1.5 * (1 - Math.exp(-d / 40)))
                                        : inside(Tlow) * Math.exp(-d / 35);
    }
    if (T > hi) {
      const d = T - hi;
      return highMode === "Decomposition" ? inside(hi) * Math.exp(d / 60)
                                          : inside(hi) * Math.exp(-d / 70);
    }
    return inside(T);
  };
  return {hi, pts: d3.range(25, 501, 2).map(T => ({T, gpc: Math.max(0, g(T))}))};
}

Plot.plot({
  height: 340, marginLeft: 65, marginBottom: 50, marginTop: 30,
  x: {label: "Deposition temperature (°C) →", domain: [25, 500]},
  y: {label: "↑ GPC (relative)", domain: [0, 3], grid: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.rectX([{x1: Tlow, x2: windowPts.hi}], {x1: "x1", x2: "x2", y1: 0, y2: 3, fill: "#8C8C8C", fillOpacity: 0.15}),
    Plot.text([{x: (Tlow + windowPts.hi) / 2, y: 2.8, label: "\"window\""}], {x: "x", y: "y", text: "label", fill: "#4D4D4D"}),
    Plot.line(windowPts.pts, {x: "T", y: "gpc", stroke: "#000000", strokeWidth: 2, clip: true})
  ]
})
```

::: {.assumptions}
**This is a schematic, not a physical model.** The functional forms outside the window are chosen only to show the direction of each effect. Use it to reason about which mechanism could explain a data set, not to fit data.
:::
:::

**A critical view of the window.** The flat plateau is a teaching idealization, and it causes two common errors:

1. *Self-limiting is not the same as temperature-independent.* For TMA/H~2~O, the GPC falls steadily with temperature over the whole useful range because the surface hydroxyl density decreases [@Puurunen2005]. The process is still self-limiting at each temperature. Set the slope slider to a negative value to see what this looks like.
2. *A plateau does not prove self-limitation.* An approximately constant GPC over some range can arise from competing effects, for example slow decomposition offset by site loss. Only dose and purge series at each temperature establish ALD behaviour.

Film properties such as crystallinity, density and impurity content also change across the "window". Crystallization onset, for example, depends on the material and the temperature, so a constant GPC does not mean a constant film [@Miikkulainen2013].

## Initial growth and nucleation

The first cycles on a new substrate rarely look like the steady state. The substrate's own surface chemistry sets how many reactive sites are available at first. Puurunen and Vandervorst classified the behaviour as **linear**, **substrate-enhanced** or **substrate-inhibited** growth, and further divided substrate-inhibited growth into two types, the second of which involves island growth [@Puurunen2004].

A simple way to capture the first three cases is a GPC that relaxes exponentially from an initial value $r\,\mathrm{GPC}_\infty$ to the steady-state value $\mathrm{GPC}_\infty$ over a characteristic number of cycles $n_0$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{GPC}(n) &= \mathrm{GPC}_\infty\left[1 + (r-1)\,e^{-n/n_0}\right] \\
d(N) &= \mathrm{GPC}_\infty\left[N + (r-1)\,n_0\left(1-e^{-N/n_0}\right)\right]
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-nucleation}

::: {.sim-box}
[Simulation 2.5: Thickness versus cycles with a nucleation transient]{.sim-title}

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof rInit = Inputs.range([0, 3], {value: 0.2, step: 0.05, label: "Initial GPC / steady-state GPC, r"})
viewof nTrans = Inputs.range([1, 100], {value: 20, step: 1, label: "Transient length, n₀ (cycles)"})
viewof gpcInf = Inputs.range([0.2, 2], {value: 1.0, step: 0.05, label: "Steady-state GPC (Å)"})
viewof nCycles = Inputs.range([10, 500], {value: 100, step: 5, label: "Cycles deposited, N"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
nuc = {
  const d = n => gpcInf * (n + (rInit - 1) * nTrans * (1 - Math.exp(-n / nTrans)));
  const pts = d3.range(0, nCycles + 1).map(n => ({n, d: d(n)}));
  const offset = (rInit - 1) * nTrans;          // asymptote: d = GPC∞ (n + offset)
  const asym = [{n: Math.max(0, -offset), d: Math.max(0, gpcInf * offset)}, {n: nCycles, d: gpcInf * (nCycles + offset)}];
  return {pts, asym, offset, dN: d(nCycles), apparent: d(nCycles) / nCycles};
}

Plot.plot({
  height: 340, marginLeft: 65, marginBottom: 50, marginTop: 30,
  x: {label: "Cycle number →"},
  y: {label: "↑ Thickness (Å)", grid: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(nuc.asym, {x: "n", y: "d", stroke: "#8C8C8C", strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
    Plot.line(nuc.pts.map(p => ({n: p.n, d: gpcInf * p.n})), {x: "n", y: "d", stroke: "#BFBFBF"}),
    Plot.line(nuc.pts, {x: "n", y: "d", stroke: "#000000", strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.dot([{n: nCycles, d: nuc.dN}], {x: "n", y: "d", r: 5, fill: "#E91C24"})
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
md`Thickness after ${nCycles} cycles: **${nuc.dN.toFixed(1)} Å** · Apparent GPC (d/N): **${nuc.apparent.toFixed(3)} Å** vs. true steady state **${gpcInf.toFixed(2)} Å** (${(100 * (nuc.apparent / gpcInf - 1)).toFixed(1)} % error)

${nuc.offset < 0 ? `Extrapolated nucleation delay (dashed line intercept): **${(-nuc.offset).toFixed(1)} cycles**` : `Extrapolated thickness offset: **+${(gpcInf * nuc.offset).toFixed(1)} Å** (substrate-enhanced)`}`
```

::: {.assumptions}
**Assumptions:** smooth, laterally uniform growth; a single exponential transient. This model does **not** reproduce the GPC overshoot of island growth (substrate-inhibited type 2), and it treats the film as continuous from the first cycle, which is false for strongly inhibited nucleation. Grey line: ideal linear growth. Dashed line: steady-state asymptote.
:::
:::

The practical lesson is that **a single thickness divided by a single cycle count is a biased GPC estimate.** Measure several cycle numbers and take the slope of the linear part instead. The bias is largest for thin films, which are exactly the films where ALD is usually chosen.

## Check your understanding

::: {.quiz}
Doubling the TMA pulse time raises film thickness by 30 %, with everything else unchanged. What is the most defensible conclusion?

- [ ] The process is below the ALD window.
- [x] The TMA step is not self-limiting under these conditions; either it is undersaturated or there is a non-self-limiting contribution, and a full dose series is needed to tell which.
- [ ] The water half-reaction is undersaturated.
- [ ] The process is ALD; a 30 % change is within normal reactor variability.

::: {.explanation}
One pair of points cannot tell undersaturation (the GPC will plateau at longer pulses) apart from a decomposition or CVD component (the GPC keeps rising). Nothing here tests the water step or the temperature.
:::
:::

::: {.quiz}
Why is the TMA/H~2~O growth per cycle well below one monolayer of Al~2~O~3~?

- [ ] Purges are never complete, so some material is removed every cycle.
- [ ] The water step partially etches the film.
- [x] Steric hindrance from the remaining methyl ligands, and the limited number of reactive surface sites, cap how much Al can adsorb per cycle.
- [ ] As-deposited ALD alumina is highly porous.

::: {.explanation}
The GPC is set by how many precursor molecules fit and react on the surface in one half-cycle. Ligand size (steric hindrance) and site density are the two limiting factors [@Puurunen2005].
:::
:::

::: {.quiz}
A colleague claims a process is "true ALD" because its GPC is constant between 150 and 250 °C. What is wrong with this argument?

- [ ] Nothing; a flat window is the standard proof of ALD.
- [x] A plateau in temperature neither proves nor is required for self-limitation; only dose and purge saturation tests establish it.
- [ ] The window must span at least 200 °C.
- [ ] GPC must increase with temperature in a true ALD process.

::: {.explanation}
Self-limiting processes can have temperature-dependent GPC (TMA/H~2~O is the standard example). A flat region can also arise from competing non-ideal effects. Saturation is tested in dose, not in temperature.
:::
:::

::: {.quiz}
A 50-cycle film is 3.0 nm thick. The steady-state GPC is known to be 1.0 Å. Assuming growth is linear after an abrupt nucleation delay, how long is the delay?

- [ ] 10 cycles
- [x] 20 cycles
- [ ] 30 cycles
- [ ] 50 cycles

::: {.explanation}
30 Å = 1.0 Å × (50 − n~delay~), so n~delay~ = 20 cycles. The apparent GPC from this single film (0.6 Å) would underestimate the true value by 40 %.
:::
:::

::: {.quiz}
A TMA/H~2~O process has a GPC of 1.1 Å, and one layer of Al~2~O~3~ is about 2.9 Å thick. A student concludes that the TMA half-reaction is undersaturated, because a saturated half-reaction should give a full monolayer. What is wrong with this reasoning?

- [ ] Nothing; the TMA dose should be increased until the GPC reaches 2.9 Å.
- [ ] The water half-reaction must be undersaturated instead.
- [x] Saturation means no further uptake, not full coverage. Steric crowding by the remaining methyl groups and the finite –OH density cap a saturated cycle at roughly 30–40 % of a monolayer.
- [ ] GPC is measured in Å/cycle, so it cannot be compared with a layer thickness.

::: {.explanation}
A saturated half-cycle stops when every remaining –OH is consumed or shielded by ligands, which happens well before a full layer of Al is adsorbed [@Barry2022; @Puurunen2005]. Increasing the dose beyond saturation does not raise the GPC.
:::
:::

## Further reading

- @George2010: a broad overview of ALD chemistries and mechanisms.
- @Puurunen2005: the definitive case study of TMA/H~2~O surface chemistry and of GPC-limiting factors.
- @Johnson2014: a short, accessible review from fundamentals to applications.
